title: Alerting
subtitle: Multi-window multi-burn-rate SLO alerting, alert fatigue prevention, and automated runbook triage.
keyTakeaways: Page humans only on actionable, user-facing symptom breaches (SLO burn rate); route cause-based or slow-burning saturation warnings to async tickets.
Multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerting pairs a long window (e.g., 1h) with a short confirmation window (e.g., 5m) to achieve fast detection and instant reset once an outage resolves.
Combat alert fatigue via deduplication, hierarchical inhibition (suppressing 50 microservice alerts when the core database or network switch is down), and mandatory runbook links.
architectureDiagram:
Incoming Error Spike

          +---> [Long Window:  1h Burn Rate > 14.4x] ---+     (2% budget      (PagerDuty)
                (Confirms statistical significance)            burned in 1h)

          +---> [Slow Burn: 6h & 30m Burn Rate > 6x] -------> [AND Gate] ---> PAGE / WARN
          +---> [Crawl Burn: 3d & 6h Burn Rate > 1x] -------> [AND Gate] ---> JIRA TICKET

sections.heading: Multi-Window, Multi-Burn-Rate Alerting Mechanics
sections.body: Static threshold alerts (e.g., `error_rate > 1% for 5m`) suffer from either poor precision (false positives on brief blips) or poor recall (missing a steady 0.5% error leak that exhausts a 99.9% monthly budget in 6 days). Google SRE's **Burn Rate** model measures how fast the service is consuming its 30-day error budget relative to a sustainable $1\times$ rate.
bullets: Burn Rate Definition: A burn rate of $1\times$ consumes 100% of the 30-day error budget in exactly 30 days. A burn rate of $14.4\times$ consumes 2% of the entire monthly budget in just 1 hour (exhausting 100% in 50 hours).

Why Two Windows (1h AND 5m) Are Required: Alerting solely on a 1-hour window means that after a 10-minute severe outage is fixed, the 1-hour average remains elevated for another 50 minutes, keeping the alert falsely firing.

Short Window Reset: Requiring *both* the 1-hour window AND the 5-minute window to exceed the $14.4\times$ burn threshold ensures the alert fires within minutes of onset and resolves within 5 minutes of recovery.

codeSnippet.title: Google SRE Multi-Window Multi-Burn-Rate Alert Rule (99.9% SLO)
codeSnippet.code:
# For a 99.9% SLO, allowed error fraction = 0.001
# 14.4x burn rate threshold = 14.4 * 0.001 = 0.0144 (1.44% error rate)
groups:
  - name: slo_burn_rate_alerts
    rules:
      - alert: HighErrorBudgetBurnPage
        expr: |
          (
            service:http_errors:ratio_rate1h > (14.4 * 0.001)
            and
            service:http_errors:ratio_rate5m > (14.4 * 0.001)
          )
          or
          (
            service:http_errors:ratio_rate6h > (6 * 0.001)
            and
            service:http_errors:ratio_rate30m > (6 * 0.001)
          )
        labels:
          severity: page
        annotations:
          summary: "High SLO error budget burn on {{ $labels.service }}"
          runbook: "https://runbooks.internal/slo/{{ $labels.service }}"

sections.heading: Alert Routing, Inhibition, and Fatigue Prevention
sections.body: When an underlying shared dependency (like a NAT gateway, core Postgres cluster, or Redis shard) fails, dozens of downstream services simultaneously breach their thresholds. Without intelligent alert topology routing, on-call engineers are flooded with hundreds of redundant pages.
bullets: Alert Inhibition & Grouping: Configure Alertmanager to group alerts by `cluster` and `namespace`, and inhibit downstream application alerts when a root-cause infrastructure alert (`DatabaseClusterDown`) is active.

Every Page Must Be Actionable: If an on-call engineer receives a page, looks at the graph, and goes back to sleep ('Oh, that always spikes during nightly ETL'), the alert must be deleted or converted into a non-paging ticket.

Automated Context Enrichment: Attach recent deployment diffs, top failing endpoints, and exemplar trace links directly into the PagerDuty/Slack payload to shave minutes off Mean Time to Detect/Mitigate (MTTD/MTTR).

tradeOffs.pros: High precision and recall; mathematically tied to customer SLOs; resets quickly after remediation.
tradeOffs.cons: Harder for junior engineers to intuit PromQL ratios compared to simple static thresholds; requires pre-computed recording rules.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Production Tier-0 and Tier-1 services with defined availability and latency SLOs.

tradeOffs.pros: Simple to configure and understand; works even on zero-traffic background workers.
tradeOffs.cons: High false-positive rate (CPU at 90% during GC or batch compression may have zero user impact), causing alert fatigue.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Stateful storage disk space (`disk_free < 15%`), certificate expiration, and dead-letter queue growth.

interviewTip: Explain the difference between a 'Page' (wake a human at 3 AM because customers are actively burning >2% of the monthly error budget in an hour) and a 'Ticket' (handle during business hours because a slow burn will exhaust budget in 10 days).
